articles.title: Emmys 2026: Memorable moments and what you didn't see on TV
articles.summary: Backstage, the winners continued the celebrations off-screen and addressed some of the ceremony's most viral moments.
articles.body:
Welsh actor Matthew Rhys and US actress Jean Smart made Emmy Awards history during TV's biggest night in Hollywood this year, which brought out stars from the small screen, film, sport and music.

Hosted by Law & Order SVU star Mariska Hargitay - the first woman to host in 15 years - the ceremony was packed with cameos from celebrities, emotional speeches, touching tributes and plenty of banter.

Backstage, the winners continued their celebrations offscreen and answered questions about their wins and some of the ceremony's most viral moments.

Here's a look at some of the viral moments as well as some of the other bits and pieces the BBC captured behind the scenes at the show.

Widow's Bay team reflect on being sleeper hit

The cast and crew behind Apple TV's sleeper hit celebrated the supernatural TV comedy's popular first season - which nabbed six wins on Monday after winning another eight at the Creative Arts Emmys earlier this month.

Asked about the show being relatively small and unknown to some audiences, the cast and creators spoke backstage with gratitude for the grassroots efforts to promote the show through word-of-mouth early on.

Main story: Rhys lands historic double Emmys win

"All the people online talking about it, or viewers, or people just tweeting about it, truly like it. That really got the word to spread, and we're so grateful," said writer and creator Katie Dippold.

Rhys quipped that those people were "predominantly our parents".

"I honestly think we're just happy that everyone reacted to the scripts the way we did when we read them, and that's all to thanks to this team," Rhys said.

He said the series was on a "giddy ascent" ahead of the Emmys. Dippold joked that she was terrified thinking that the show might get even more attention after all their Emmy wins.

Matthew Rhys jokes about rivalry with partner Keri Russell

Welsh actor Matthew Rhys refused to go backstage and talk with reporters until he found out whether Hiro Murai, the Widow's Bay director, won in the directing category (he did).

When he finally made his way to the microphone, Rhys specifically called on the BBC for the first question.

"The BBC, surely!" he said, before reflecting on making history and becoming the first person to win two Emmy awards for best lead actor in the same year - for his role in the psychological thriller The Beast In Me as well as his role in Widow's Bay.

"At the moment, I genuinely can't quite believe what's just happened," he said. "I hope to reflect on it tomorrow."

He also teased the friendly competition between him and his partner, actress Keri Russell, who was up for an Emmy for her role in The Diplomat this year.

"It's not great. I bet a lot of money on myself. The kids ran a book," he joked, adding: "It's going to be a rough week for her. I'm sorry. I don't know if I am."

He joked, waving around the trophy, that Russell was his better half and "always the class act".

"She's always really the winner, if I'm perfectly honest."

Kate O'Flynn wants to see your Halloween costumes

Kate O'Flynn, another star of Widow's Bay, told reporters backstage that she was "completely gobsmacked" and "on top of the world" by her win in the spooky comedy, which centres on the strange happenings of a haunted New England island.

She said that her character - Patricia, the assistant to Mayor Tom Loftis (played by Matthew Rhys) - had an "awkwardness", "bravery and humour" that resonated with audiences.

"I think everyone just has felt like Patricia in that way," she said.

O'Flynn said she was pleasantly surprised by "an army" of people who turned up dressed as her character at this year's DragonCon.

"So I'm excited to see Halloween and all the antlers come out and take over the world," she joked to reporters.

Speaking to the BBC, the British actress had a message for everyone back home: "Just to our family and friends, we did it. It's great. I don't know what to say. I don't know."

A bustling 'backstage' where statuettes are engraved

What did the show look like behind the scenes?

The BBC had a team at the Peacock Theater in downtown Los Angeles, which was shut down to traffic and onlookers as celebrities in black cars took over.

Droves of celebrity handlers dressed in black - from security staff to publicists - were posted throughout the area - which also sits across from Crypto.com Arena, the home to the LA Lakers. While the ceremony and red carpet is mostly confined to the Peacock Theater, the set-up around it is vast.

Next door at the JW Marriott hotel, ballrooms were converted into press workspaces where celebrities and their teams milled about throughout the ceremony, reuniting cast-mates who hadn't seen each other since they wrapped filming.

The road to this area was long, windy and done on foot. Once a winner accepted their prize on TV, they were taken across the street to get their awards engraved, take photos and chat with reporters.

They were escorted through a series of covered spaces, where they popped into one ballroom specifically for photos, another to speak with print and digital media, and then another section cordoned off just for TV interviews.

This area was also where winners got their awards engraved. Dozens of golden Emmy statues were set up on tables here, which passers-by (including yours truly) can gawk at and take photos of.

So, in every way, "backstage" isn't really "backstage" at the Emmys. It's more like "next door".

An Emmys 'statue' walks the red (blue?) carpet

In a sea of glamorous gowns and tuxedoes, Hacks star Megan Stalter, who was nominated for best comedy supporting actress, arrived on the Emmys blue carpet dressed as an Emmy statuette.

The actress, who has repeatedly turned heads with her red-carpet looks, gilded herself gold body paint and angel wings for the look, and held up an enormous model of the spherical atom that features as part of each statuette.

Stalter dodged questions about what inspired the look, telling reporters that she and her stylist just threw it together and that her co-star Paul W Downs airbrushed her himself.

Allison Janney's shocked face becomes a meme

When Allison Janney's name was announced as the winner for best supporting actress in drama, the camera panned to The Diplomat star with her mouth open and both hands cupping the sides of her face.

She remained for several seconds before getting up, still surprised, and covering her mouth in shock. "Oh my God," the fictional president was seen mouthing as she made her way to the stage.

Rival programme The Pitt flooded nominations for Outsanding Supporting Actress in a Drama Series, meaning that the medical drama seemed poised to have one of its stars take home the prize.

So Janney, who plays the US president in The Diplomat, a political drama, told reporters backstage that she was "genuinely shocked" by her win.

"We really didn't think it was going to go my way. So I felt just excited and relaxed," she said, because she was "100% sure I wasn't gonna win".

Host Mariska Hargitay calls on Taylor Swift for skit

Host Mariska Hargitay called on a handful of celebrities during her hosting debut, including Taylor Swift, Jalen Brunson and Broadway star Andrew Rannells.

The Law & Order SVU star opened the show with a musical number based on Joan Jett and the Blackheart's I Love Rock & Roll, name-checking many of the shows and stars of the night, while singing "I love TV screens".

NBA star Jalen Brunson made a cameo - which was a nod to Hargitay's love of the New York Knicks basketball team. Later, in a pre-recorded skit, Hargitay and her co-stars from Law & Order SVU tried to solve the mystery of whether Taylor Swift would appear at the Emmys.

Swift did the appear, joining in as a character trying to solve the case, which took viewers on a tour of the nominees and Swift's album and personal life.

The skit closed with Hargitay, Swift and one of her cats - who is named Olivia Benson after Hargitay's character on the Law & Order series.

DTF St Louis star says all the mothers are watching

DTF St Louis star Arlan Ruf, who plays David Harbour's son on the dark comedy miniseries, joked about the primary demographic who were fans of the HBO series - which centres on a murder connected to a dating app.

"I don't know a lot of my friends are watching it," he said cheekily, but added that their mothers were.

Ruf added that his friends' mothers had been telling him how great the programme was - nodding to the large female audience for true crime.

"So every friend's mom I know is watching," he said.

articles.title: Bill Gates is very impressed with China's AI growth that US government has been warning its companies about, says...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Bill Gates recently praised the rapid progress of China's artificial intelligence industry at a time when the US government has been warning American .
articles.body: Bill Gates recently praised the rapid progress of China's artificial intelligence industry at a time when the US government has been warning American companies about China's growing strength in AI. “Depending on how you measure it, both China and the United States each have four or more institutions whose models are capable of maintaining state-of-the-art levels. The gap between the top-scoring model and the other seven leading models is actually not that large,” Gates said in an interview in New York recently. His comments came as the Gates Foundation announced at least $1 billion in AI funding over the next two years, aimed at bringing AI tools to poorer countries in areas including healthcare, education and agriculture.Bill Gates says China and US are in AI 'super competition'During the interview, Bill Gates was asked about the progress of Chinese open-source AI models and gave a strong assessment of the country's development. Gates said China and the US each have four or more institutions with models capable of maintaining state-of-the-art performance, while also describing the two countries as being in a “super competition” over AI talent and computing power. He, however, did not name the institutions.Gates also said the world's eight leading large language models have all moved beyond the best performance seen about four months earlier. He described the AI race between China and the US as a “super competition”, with both countries competing for talent and computing power.Bill Gates says China's AI progress could benefit poorer countriesBill Gates said the competition between the two countries could have an unexpected benefit for developing nations. He said the availability of more high-performing models could give low-income countries, including those in Africa, access to cheaper AI tools.Open-source AI models, he added, provide “great flexibility.” Gates said some African countries already borrow servers from Chinese partners to run AI models remotely. He said the delay in communication is still low enough for many uses.He suggested that African countries should focus their own limited resources on areas where local development is most important, such as language support and local data.Bill Gates proposes 5% of China and US computing power for poorer nationsGates also proposed that China and the US each provide around 5% of their data-centre computing power for use by poorer countries. He compared the idea to foreign aid and said the computing resources could support healthcare, agriculture and education.“If you're just answering questions about health or farming, the token consumption isn't that high,” Gates said. He argued that the world should establish a basic level of AI access so that people everywhere can benefit from the technology.Gates Foundation commits $1 billion to AI equityThe Gates Foundation said it will invest at least $1 billion over the next two years to improve access to AI in poorer parts of the world. About $400 million will go toward healthcare. The foundation wants to support tools that can help clinicians review reports and spot symptoms that may have been missed.Another $400 million will focus on education, including tools that can help teachers redesign lessons around areas where students struggle. Around $100 million will support agriculture, including AI tools that can give farmers advice on weather, pests and fertilisation. Another $100 million will go toward building language datasets that are currently poorly represented in AI systems.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: A Texas farmer stopped planting cotton and sent his sheep to solar farms; the switch turned a potential $200,000 loss into $300,000 profit
articles.summary: US News: Chad Raines, a fourth-generation Texas cotton farmer, stopped planting cotton after years of losses and found a very different way to make a living fr.
articles.body: Chad Raines, a fourth-generation Texas cotton farmer, stopped planting cotton after years of losses and found a very different way to make a living from his land and livestock. Instead of relying on crops, he began moving sheep between solar farms, where the animals graze on grass growing beneath and around the panels. The change transformed the economics of his farm. According to CBS News, Raines estimated a cotton crop would have cost him nearly $200,000 in losses, while his sheep-grazing operation brought in close to $300,000 in profit.How did a Texas farmer turn sheep and solar farms into a $300,000 profitRaines had spent generations in the cotton business, but the numbers were becoming increasingly difficult to justify. According to CBS News, several years of poor harvests and low cotton prices left the family unable to make progress. Debt continued to build, forcing Raines to consider an option far from the traditional row-crop farming his family had followed for four generations.The solution was solar grazing. Raines began providing sheep to solar companies so the animals could feed on vegetation around their panels. Instead of using the flock simply to produce meat, he was being paid for the work the sheep performed on the solar sites.As reported by the Western Producer, Raines did not plant a single cotton seed in the 2024 growing season. He instead rented most of his Texas farmland to a neighbour and spent his time taking his sheep to solar farms. He had agreements with five solar companies, making the grazing work more profitable than growing cotton.What made solar farms useful for sheep grazingSolar farms need vegetation kept under control so grass and other plants do not interfere with their equipment or make maintenance more difficult. Traditionally, this work can involve machinery and workers repeatedly cutting vegetation.Sheep offer a different approach. They can move between rows of panels and feed directly on the grass. One such example of a solar farm is the large Enel North America solar farm near Waco, Texas, with more than one million panels, where sheep are used to manage vegetation. According to CBS, Site manager Adam Sotirakopoulos said that the animals could continue working in conditions when machines might be less practical, including rain, mud and at night.The Western Producer reported that managed grazing can also reduce costs for solar companies. Silicon Ranch, a Tennessee-based solar company, said it saves about 20% in operating expenses on a site with managed grazing. The company noted that paying shepherds can be less expensive than keeping mowing crews and machinery working continuously.How sheep grazing became a profitable farm businessRaines did not depend entirely on grazing payments. According to The Western Producer, he also began selling lamb meat to a restaurant supplier. Together, the solar grazing income and lamb sales helped him make about $300,000 in profit. He said the solar payments covered his expenses, including labour and about $2,000 a month spent on food for guard dogs. His son also returned to the farm to help with the growing operation.As reported by CBS News, Raines was grazing about 6,000 sheep across 20,000 acres. The scale gave the family a business that could also provide work for his sons, giving the farm a possible future beyond cotton.The arrangement also changed the nature of the farmer's income. Instead of growing a crop and then accepting whatever price the market offered, grazing contracts gave him a more predictable payment for a service. Other farmers described solar grazing as a way to create steadier income during difficult agricultural years.Solar grazing is spreading across American farmlandRaines is part of a much larger shift. The Western Producer reported that sheep grazed on more than 129,000 acres of US solar sites in October 2024, compared with 15,000 acres in 2021. The number of sheep working on solar sites also rose from about 80,000 to more than 113,000 between January and October of that year.According to CyberGuy, sheeps can replace gas-powered mowing crews, reducing maintenance costs and emissions. It also highlighted the Texas operation as an example of how grazing contracts can create another source of income for farmers.For solar companies, the appeal is practical. Sheep naturally eat the vegetation that would otherwise need to be controlled. For farmers, the same animals can generate income without requiring them to plant another crop.Importance of this shift for American farmers The change comes at a difficult time for American agriculture. The Western Producer reported that US cotton futures had fallen nearly 40% over 2 years, while American exports had also declined as cheaper Brazilian supplies and weaker Chinese demand affected the market.Nearly 40% of small and mid-sized US farms operated at a loss in the previous year, according to a 2024 US Department of Agriculture report. For farmers facing high costs and falling returns, finding an additional income source can make the difference between keeping a farm operating and leaving agriculture altogether.For Raines, that choice was particularly stark. Solar grazing gave him another route, turning a difficult farming year into a profitable one while keeping his family involved in agriculture.The result is a unique partnership between livestock and renewable energy. Rows of solar panels provide the setting, while sheep provide the maintenance, and farmers gain an income that traditional cotton farming could no longer reliably provide.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: State pension likely to top £13,000 a year as UK wage growth slows to 3.9%
articles.summary: The rise has reignited the debate about the state pension's long-term affordability and generational fairness.
articles.body:
The state pension is expected to top £13,000 a year, reigniting the debate about its long-term affordability and generational fairness.

The full, flat-rate state pension is expected to rise by £488 a year in April, based on the latest official earnings figure released on Tuesday.

The so-called triple lock pension policy guarantees that the state pension will increase by either average wage growth, inflation or 2.5% - whichever is highest.

Labour made a manifesto pledge to keep the triple lock until 2029, however economists have warned about the cost of the policy ahead of the Budget although pensioner groups say many people still face poverty in old age.

The triple lock was designed to ensure the value of the state pension was not overtaken by the increase in the cost of living or the incomes of working people.

Although the state pension age is rising to 67, the cost to the government has risen considerably too. Forecasts suggest state pension spending, already at £154bn this year, could go up by a further £600m a year by 2029-30.

The policy is "crazy," Ruth Curtice, the chief executive of the Resolution Foundation think tank, told the BBC.

The triple lock is creating a "ratchet effect" where "pensioners' living standards grow even faster than just a typical worker," she added.

"Pensioners have seen living standards grow three times more than typical workers over the last 20 years."

Jonathan Cribb, deputy director of Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) think tank, said: "Each increase in spending builds upon the last and so the long-run cost is substantial but very uncertain."

The state pension is expected to match wage growth in the next calculation and is likely to be higher than the rate of inflation.

Average wage growth, including bonuses, stood at 3.9% between May and July, according to the Office for National Statistics (ONS) , down from 4.2% between April and June.

But it is higher than average pay growth, not including bonuses, which rose by 3.5%.

the flat-rate state pension - for those who reached state pension age after April 2016 – will likely be £250.70 a week, or £13,036.40 a year. That would be an increase of £488

the old basic state pension - for those who reached state pension age before April 2016 – will likely be £192.10 a week, or £9,989.20 a year, an increase of £374.40

Pensioner groups have said older people face significant cost of living pressures, such as high energy bills and the state pension itself remained relatively small compared with state provision across Europe.

The Today Debate: Can we afford the pensions triple lock?

Why Gen Z are planning for life without a state pension

What is the triple lock and how much is the state pension worth?

Almost 13 million people receive the state pension in the UK. If it does rise by 3.9%, it would take the flat-rate state pension above the personal allowance of £12,570 and therefore be liable for income tax.

The government said it has recommitted to exempting people whose only income is the state pension from tax.

The Labour government - when Rachel Reeves was chancellor - promised that pensioners who rely solely on the state pension would not be required to complete a tax return, nor be chased to pay.

When asked by the BBC on Tuesday morning, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds refused to confirm that pensioners reliant on the state pension will be exempted from paying income tax.

Later, pensions minister Torsten Bell, said: "In line with the commitment made at Budget 2025, pensioners who only just the exceed the personal allowance will not pay small amounts of tax in this parliament which we know is an administrative burden.

"The chancellor will set out further details on how that commitment will be delivered at the Budget."

Analysis by consultants LCP suggested that only one in 16 pensioners would benefit under the government's pledge, saving about £91 each a year.

The majority of pensioners have additional pension income and so pay income tax already.

"The government's plans to address this point are a mess," said Sir Steve Webb, a partner at LCP and a former Liberal Democrat pensions minister.

Prior to the government saying it had recommitted to its pledge on tax and pensions, shadow chancellor Andrew Griffith said: "People living on nothing but their state pension are now facing a tax bill for the first time ever.

"Many will spend the last years of their lives filing tax returns or hanging on HMRC telephone helplines."

The ONS also published figures on the UK labour force.

While the unemployment rate was unchanged at 4.9%, the number of vacancies and employees on payrolls fell in recent months.

articles.title: Objectors protest against Microsoft's major Leeds data centre
articles.summary: On Saturday around 250 people gathered for a protest in Millennium Square against the development.
articles.body:
More than 42,000 people have signed a petition objecting to a Microsoft data centre near Leeds.

Microsoft is continuing to face opposition to the scheme at the former Skelton Grange power station site in Stourton.

Supporters of the petition have raised concerns over the amount of water and energy it would use, though Microsoft has said it is committed to being "carbon negative [and] water positive" by 2030.

On Saturday around 250 people gathered for a protest against the development in Millennium Square in Leeds organised by action group No Leeds Data Centre.

Campaigner Kate Pearson told the Local Democracy Reporting Service : "I don't think we necessarily need such massive data centres that cause such environmental harm".

Campaign organiser Lianne Marie Mease said she was was worried about the impact on wildlife during building work at the disused power station site.

"This specific development here in Leeds, the size of it is far bigger than it needs to be," she said.

"The area that it's being built in was allowed to re-wild over 32 years, and clearing that site is going to impact species that are rare or at risk to Leeds."

Microsoft said the complex, given planning permission in April, would power digital services for communities, businesses and the public sector.

A spokesperson for the company said it was working "working closely" with local authorities through the planning process.

They added: "The proposed facility would be air cooled for more than 95% of the time, we match all our energy use with renewable energy in the UK, and Microsoft remains committed to our goals of becoming carbon negative, water positive and zero waste by 2030."

Leeds City Council previously said approval of the planning application was in line with national legislation and policies.

Microsoft's scheme includes three data centre buildings housing computer servers, along with a warehouse with up to 161,000 sq ft (15,000 sq m), of floorspace.

A public consultation was held on the development, which includes the installation of power connections, cooling chimneys and back-up generators.

articles.title: US court blocks Trump administration's four-year visa rule for international students and researchers
articles.summary: US & Canada News News: In a major reprieve for international students, researchers, academics and foreign journalists, a US federal district court has blocked the Trump admi.
articles.body: In a major reprieve for international students, researchers, academics and foreign journalists, a US federal district court has blocked the Trump administration from implementing a new rule that would replace the longstanding ‘duration of status’ system with fixed periods of admission.The district court’s order means that the new framework, which was scheduled to take effect on Sept 15, cannot be implemented for now. The existing duration-of-status framework therefore remains in place nationwide.US District Judge F Dennis Saylor IV of the District of Massachusetts on Monday granted preliminary relief to organisations representing higher education institutions, international educators, journalists and others. The district court postponed the effective date of the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) final rule, while litigation challenging its legality continues.TOI had earlier analysed the new rule.Also read: Trump administration limits visa tenure of students to a fixed period of four years and limits academic flexibilityInternational students were allowed to stay in the US, as long as they were studying. The new rule eliminated this ‘duration of status’ concept and subjected international students (F1 visa holders), exchange visitors (J visa holders) and representatives of foreign media to fixed periods of stay. In a double whammy, the new rule also introduced new restrictions on academic flexibility for international students.The rule was challenged in the district court by the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, NAFSA: Association of International Educators, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, the American Federation of Teachers, The NewsGuild-CWA, and others.The ruling is particularly significant for international students pursuing lengthy or evolving academic programmes, including doctoral candidates, as well as researchers and scholars whose work may extend beyond a fixed admission period.What the rule sought to changeUnder the duration of status system, international students admitted on F-1 visas may generally remain in the US while pursuing a full course of study and authorised practical training, provided they maintain their immigration status. J-1 exchange visitors, including researchers, professors, teachers and trainees, are similarly admitted for the duration of their approved programme or activity.The system has been in place for decades. The district court noted that duration of status for F visa holders dates back to 1978, while the corresponding system for J visa holders was introduced in 1985.DHS's final rule, published on July 17, sought to replace this arrangement with fixed periods of admission. F-1 and J-1 visa holders would generally be subject to a maximum four-year admission period, regardless of the anticipated length of their educational programme or research.Those requiring additional time would have to apply to US Citizenship and Immigration Services (USCIS) for an extension of stay, generally using Form I-539. The rule also provided for a 240-day limit for foreign media representatives holding I visas, subject to an extension process.For students, the proposed change would have had consequences beyond the need to seek extensions. The rule placed restrictions on academic flexibility. Graduate students would generally be prohibited from changing their educational objectives or transferring between institutions, subject to limited exceptions for extenuating circumstances. International students would also generally be required to pursue a subsequent programme at a higher educational level, preventing them from undertaking another programme at the same or a lower level while retaining F-1 status.The rule also reduced the post-completion departure period for F and J visa holders who completed their programmes early to 30 days.District court questions DHS's justificationJudge Saylor's order found that the plaintiffs were likely to succeed in their challenge under the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires agencies to act reasonably, consider relevant evidence and explain the connection between the facts they identify and the policies they adopt.The district court identified four principal deficiencies in DHS's rulemaking.First, it said DHS had failed to conduct a reasoned assessment of the costs and benefits of the new framework. In particular, the agency had not adequately accounted for the potential impact on international student enrolment, research, teaching and the travel of foreign journalists.Second, DHS had not meaningfully considered less burdensome alternatives to replacing duration of status.Third, the agency had failed to respond adequately to significant public comments raising concerns about the rule's consequences.Fourth, it found that DHS had not demonstrated a rational connection between the rule and its stated objectives of protecting national security and preventing fraud and abuse.“The use of such labels does not, however, give DHS license to ignore its statutory obligations,” the judge said, referring to the agency's reliance on national security and border protection.In his order the judge also questioned whether the weak connection between the rule and its stated rationales raised concerns about other, undisclosed objectives, including “greater government control over academic institutions and the press”.The district court stressed that its role was not to decide whether the Trump administration had adopted a wise or unwise policy. Its task was to determine whether DHS had complied with the law when promulgating the regulation.Impact on international students and US universitiesThe ruling comes at a time when US universities are heavily dependent on international students, particularly at the graduate level and in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) disciplines.The district court noted that there are approximately 1.6 million individuals in F status and about 500,000 in J status. More than half of all international students major in STEM fields, according to data cited in the order.The judge also highlighted the contribution of international students and scholars to American research, innovation and economic growth. The order referred to evidence that international student alumni had founded 143 of 582 billion-dollar US start-ups, or 25%.The potential impact of the rule was reflected in comments submitted during the rulemaking process. A survey of 1,039 current international students, cited by NAFSA, found that 49% said they would not have enrolled in the US had duration of status been replaced with a fixed admission period. A separate survey of 611 prospective students found that 16% fewer respondents said they were likely to enrol under such a system.The new rule adversely impacted Indian students, as they are the largest contingent of international students. According to the latest Open Doors Report, during the academic year 2024-25, there were 3.6 lakh Indian students in the US constituting nearly 31% of the total number of 11 lakh international students. Experts point out that while the numbers of new students from India is falling, the cohort of Indian students will continue to be significant.The district court also noted that doctoral programmes frequently extend beyond four years. Citing evidence submitted during the rulemaking process, it said the median completion time for doctoral programmes was nearly six years, while bachelor's degrees also often took more than four years. The uncertainty created by the extension process could therefore discourage students from choosing the US, the district court found.The order recorded examples of harm that had allegedly begun even before the rule took effect. Two international students at the University of Wisconsin-Madison and 32 at the University of Maryland, Baltimore, had withdrawn from their programmes, according to evidence cited by the plaintiffs. The University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee had also reported a 42% decline in applications from international students in the academic year in question.The order of district court states that the new system could allow a DHS official, acting on “limited and vague criteria” and without any possibility of appeal, to cut short the academic, research or teaching activities of a non-US citizen. An international student who was only one credit short of graduation, for instance, could be required to leave the US without a degree and without any recourse, the judge said. The resulting uncertainty, it added, would have an obvious deterrent effect on student enrolment.The district court said the requirement to seek extensions from USCIS, where decisions would be discretionary and unappealable, could lead students to choose countries offering more predictable routes to completing their studies.Concerns over academic freedom and press freedomThe district court also questioned the effect of the rule on academic flexibility.It observed that international students may legitimately change their research interests, alter their academic objectives, transfer institutions or pursue joint degrees. A fixed system that restricts such changes could disrupt established programmes and impose significant burdens on universities.The order referred to concerns raised by institutions that they were already being forced to reconsider joint and combined degree programmes for international students. It also noted that some students had cancelled international research or conference travel because of uncertainty surrounding the new rule.The proposed 240-day limit for I visa holders raised separate concerns about foreign journalists' ability to develop sources and report effectively in the US. The judge in his order also expressed concern that the system could be abused to punish individuals whose viewpoints or research were disfavoured by officials, or to penalise institutions considered undesirable.Economic and administrative costsDHS had acknowledged that the rule would impose significant compliance costs. Its final analysis projected quantified costs of between $443.1 million and $448.6 million overall, including costs to applicants, universities and other affected parties.The district court, however, found that the agency had not adequately weighed those costs against the asserted benefits.The judge also criticised DHS's response to concerns about a decline in international enrolment. When commenters cited evidence that the new system could deter students, the agency offered no countervailing quantitative study, the order said. Instead, it suggested that universities might fill vacancies left by students who chose not to enrol with other qualified applicants.The district court rejected that as an adequate response to concerns about the loss of highly qualified international graduate students, particularly in fields such as science and technology.It further noted that DHS had not sufficiently explained why existing mechanisms, including the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS), could not be used more effectively to address fraud and national security concerns without replacing duration of status.Why the relief applies nationwideThe plaintiffs had sought relief that would prevent the rule from taking effect. Judge Saylor concluded that the court had authority under Section 705 of the APA to postpone the effective date of the regulation.The judge considered whether relief should be limited to the organisations and institutions represented by the plaintiffs or should apply nationwide.The plaintiffs represented almost 600 public and private institutions, while more than 000 higher-education institutions operate in the US. Limiting relief to the represented parties, the district court said, could require parallel regulatory regimes and repeated, potentially inconsistent determinations about which students and institutions fell within the order’s scope. The situation would be particularly complicated because students regularly transfer institutions or pursue joint degrees. A nationwide order, the judge concluded, would prevent the “chaos and confusion” that a party-specific order would inevitably generate.The district court also held that the final rule directly threatened the benefits provided by international students, researchers and journalists “to the substantial detriment of the American public”. Postponing the rule would not harm the public interest, the judge said, because the measure was not reasonably related to any legitimate DHS objective.The district court therefore postponed the effective date of the final rule in its entirety.However, the order did not finally strike down or vacate the rule. The plaintiffs' requests for vacatur and other final relief were denied without prejudice to being renewed. The underlying litigation will continue.Relief welcomed by international education groupsMiriam Feldblum, president and CEO of the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, welcomed the decision, saying it recognised the serious and irreparable harm the rule could cause to international students, scholars, higher education institutions and the US economy.“While the case continues, this relief preserves the longstanding system that enables our colleges and universities — and our country — to attract, educate, and retain global talent,” she said.Fanta Aw, executive director and CEO of NAFSA: Association of International Educators, said the nationwide relief was an important step towards preserving a fair and predictable system for international students and scholars.“At a time when countries around the world are competing for talent, the US should be strengthening our ability to attract the best and brightest, not creating new barriers to it,” Fanta Aw said.Randi Weingarten, president of the American Federation of Teachers, said the preliminary injunction demonstrated that the administration's proposed limits on the time international scholars had to complete their studies were arbitrary and hostile.The UAW Higher Education Department also welcomed the ruling, saying it was a victory for researchers, graduate workers and postdoctoral fellows who contribute to scientific discoveries and teaching in the US. The department said many of its members were international students and scholars working in fields including medicine, engineering and climate science, and that the stability provided by the duration ofstatus system was essential to their work.The district court's order preserves that system for now, but the legal challenge to DHS's attempt to replace it with fixed periods of admission remains pending.

articles.title: Material found at several sites: Suspected sabotage causes major Dutch rail outage during rush hour
articles.summary: Europe News: A major outage disrupted parts of the Dutch railway network during Tuesday’s morning rush hour after materials were deliberately placed on tracks at s.
articles.body: A major outage disrupted parts of the Dutch railway network during Tuesday’s morning rush hour after materials were deliberately placed on tracks at several locations, prompting infrastructure operator ProRail to treat the incident as possible sabotage.“Materials deliberately placed on the tracks have been found at several locations,” ProRail said, adding that the objects had caused track-circuit failures.According to Ukraine’s Centre for Strategic Communication and Information Security (CSCIS), the materials included pipes and other objects that were deliberately fixed to or placed on railway tracks. One train struck material left on the line but remained on the tracks, with no injuries reported, the centre said.The incidents were reported along the Utrecht-Arnhem, Amersfoort-Deventer and Gouda-Oudewater routes. The interference affected signalling and safety systems as well as some railway crossings, disrupting both train and road traffic, according to CSCIS, the Ukrainian government body that monitors and counters disinformation and information threats.National railway operator NS said services around the central cities of Zwolle, Deventer and Amersfoort were severely affected. The disruption was so extensive that the operator said it could not provide enough replacement buses for stranded passengers. It was not immediately clear when services would return to normal.There was no immediate indication of who was behind the suspected sabotage or what the motive was. CSCIS described the incident as another suspected act of Russian terrorism in the European Union, but Dutch authorities have not publicly attributed the railway disruption to Russia.The disruption came as the Dutch government was due to present its annual budget to parliament, an event that draws thousands of people to The Hague to watch the royal family travel through the city in horse-drawn carriages.Investigators were also examining whether the coordinated incidents could be connected to Prinsjesdag, the annual opening of the Dutch parliamentary year, according to CSCIS.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Gurugram hit-and-run case: Police detain driver for striking woman motorcyclist
articles.summary: The incident has sparked a broader discussion about the harassment and hostility faced by female motorcyclists.
articles.body:
Police in India have detained a man after footage appearing to show a car striking a female motorcyclist in the city of Gurugram near India's capital Delhi sparked national outrage.

The incident took place on Sunday when Shivani Chauhan was riding with a group of motorcyclists.

A video recorded by a camera mounted on her bike appears to show a white car moving close and hitting her motorcycle. Chauhan falls on to the road as her motorcycle skids away, while the car continues moving.

The clip, shared by Chauhan on Instagram, has gone viral, prompting police to open an investigation. The driver, identified as Kalyan Bainsla, has denied hitting her deliberately.

On Tuesday, Gurugram police spokesperson Sandeep Kumar confirmed to the BBC that Bainsla, a gym owner from Palwal in Haryana state, had been detained. Police said he had borrowed the car from another man.

The case was initially registered under sections of the law which deal with rash driving and acts endangering life or personal safety. Police later added "attempted murder" to the charges.

In an interview with Aaj Tak news channel , Bainsla claimed that members of the biking group had repeatedly overtaken his car before slowing down in front of it. He said he lost control near a U-turn while trying to avoid Chauhan's motorcycle.

Bainsla also said he did not initially realise that Chauhan was a woman and maintained that he had asked her and another rider to slow down.

He claimed he drove away because the motorcyclists were shouting abuses and he feared that he and his relatives would be attacked.

"Had I stopped right then, those people would have beaten us up," he told the channel.

Chauhan has disputed his account. In a video posted on Instagram after the crash, she said the car had begun following her group shortly after they started their ride.

She alleged that its occupants became hostile and asked her to stop after she told the driver to keep a safe distance. Chauhan said she continued riding because she feared the car might block her, while a friend riding behind tried to shield her motorcycle.

She also alleged that the men in the car appeared to be intoxicated. The police have not said whether alcohol tests were conducted.

But Bainsla's lawyer, Naveen Bainsla, denied the allegation, telling the ANI news agency that his client had not been drinking and was travelling with relatives. He also rejected the description of the incident as a deliberate "hit-and-run case", arguing that it was a case of negligent driving.

After Bainsla publicly denied hitting her deliberately, Chauhan posted another video on Monday night challenging his version of events.

She said the footage showed which vehicle had been moving towards the other. She also rejected his claim that he had not realised she was a woman.

Chauhan also questioned why Bainsla had not stopped to check on her. "I could have been gravely hurt or broken my bones. I could've died on the spot," she said.

Chauhan sustained minor injuries, according to reports, but her protective gear is believed to have prevented more serious harm.

The footage has prompted widespread anger online and a broader discussion about the harassment and hostility female bikers say they face on Indian roads.

Several women riders shared their experiences of being followed, filmed without consent or challenged to race, particularly when they were riding high-powered motorcycles.

Divya Sandhu, a riding coach who was involved in a similar collision a decade ago, told NDTV channel that attitudes had changed little since then.

"It's very common for people to joke about women's driving skills," she said.

Another motorcyclist, Pallavi Singh, said some women concealed their hair and wore full protective clothing partly to avoid being identified and harassed while riding.

articles.title: ‘Born without making a sound’: New docs reveal chilling details about Trump rally shooter
articles.summary: US News: Newly released FBI interview documents reviewed by the New York Post provide fresh details about Thomas Matthew Crooks, the 20-year-old gunman who att.
articles.body: Newly released FBI interview documents reviewed by the New York Post provide fresh details about Thomas Matthew Crooks, the 20-year-old gunman who attempted to assassinate then-presidential candidate Donald Trump at a campaign rally in July 2024.The documents were provided to Senate judiciary committee chairman Chuck Grassley as part of his ongoing investigation into the July 13, 2024, shooting.Crooks’ father, Matthew, told investigators that his son had been unusually quiet from childhood. “When Thomas was born he did not scream and he was always quiet from that point on,” he said, according to FBI interview notes.Matthew said he never developed a strong father-son bond with Crooks and described him as someone who rarely displayed strong emotions, seldom laughed and was difficult to read.Matthew recalled several incidents from Crooks’ childhood in which he acted out, including damaging a school desk because he was bored and wanted attention.By middle school, his parents suspected he had ADHD and were concerned about the group of children he was associating with. During his high-school years, Matthew said Crooks became increasingly quiet and reserved and developed difficulties communicating with teachers.He also recalled that Crooks frequently talked to himself, a behaviour that became more noticeable as he grew older.Despite his social difficulties, Crooks performed well academically. His father said Crooks put considerable pressure on himself because he feared he might not get into college.Crooks had expressed interest in several careers but did not appear committed to any of them. At one point, he even considered joining the military and working on nuclear submarines, although his father said he appeared attracted to the idea because he thought it would be “cool”.Matthew also told investigators that Crooks never appeared to have a romantic interest in women and repeatedly denied being gay when the subject came up.From target practice to firearms obsessionCrooks became interested in guns as a teenager and began visiting a gun club around the time of the Covid-19 pandemic.His father initially considered him a poor shot. Matthew told investigators that Crooks was initially unable to hit the paper target and that it took several years of practice before his accuracy improved.Crooks eventually became a skilled marksman and began experimenting with longer-range shooting. His father recalled him explaining that he wanted to find out how far he could shoot using basic sights.After purchasing a prism sight, Crooks became increasingly knowledgeable about adjusting and zeroing it, according to his father.His interest in firearms also extended to modifying and building equipment. Matthew told investigators that his son once attempted to make a Glock 19 using carbon-fibre plastic and household equipment.Crooks also acquired a 3D printer and built a gaming computer and a security camera using a Raspberry Pi, according to the FBI interview notes.As Crooks' interest in firearms grew, he began ordering large numbers of parts, tools and other items online, his father told investigators.He sometimes used the name “Bob Dole” as a delivery name. Matthew said the practice stemmed from Crooks' concerns after his father's bank account was compromised and fraudulent BetMGM charges appeared.Crooks apparently believed that using an assumed name would make his purchases harder to trace or his accounts harder to hack. His father tried to explain that the transactions would still be connected to the bank account being used, but Crooks continued using pseudonyms.Matthew also said his son introduced him to privacy tools and used several encrypted email services.Political views offered no clear motiveThe FBI documents also provide conflicting indications about Crooks' political interests, but his father said he did not appear strongly aligned with either major party.One person interviewed by the FBI described Crooks as interested in history and politics and said he discussed Trump, Joe Biden and other political figures, including Marco Rubio.Matthew said Crooks identified as a Republican and opposed welfare programmes and what he called “woke” ideology, but did not strongly embrace Republican politics. Instead, he preferred discussing government policy more generally and making fun of politicians.Crooks was registered as a Republican, although his father believed this was partly because of his own political affiliation. Matthew also told investigators that his son did not believe the 2020 presidential election had been stolen and was shocked by the January 6, 2021, Capitol riot.Matthew said he was surprised to discover that Crooks had donated $15 to the Progressive Turnout Project, a Democratic organising group, in 2021.The FBI documents did not establish a clear political motive for the shooting.Crooks was killed by Secret Service personnel seconds after firing at Trump from a rooftop near the rally site. Trump was grazed in the ear, while one rally attendee was killed and two others were seriously injured.Matthew told investigators that the family had struggled to understand why his son decided to attack Trump.He said Crooks had not shown obvious signs that something was wrong, leaving the family unable to identify a clear motive for the assassination attempt.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: ‘No child should be deprived of dignity’: Delhi HC allows 15-year-old rape survivor to terminate pregnancy
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has held that compelling a rape survivor to continue with a pregnancy resulting from sexual assault and forcing mother.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The Delhi High Court has held that compelling a rape survivor to continue with a pregnancy resulting from sexual assault and forcing motherhood upon her against her will would seriously impair her right to live with dignity.The court made the observation while allowing a plea filed on behalf of a 15-year-old rape survivor seeking termination of her pregnancy, which had crossed 30 weeks of gestation, news agency PTI reported.Justice Madhu Jain said the fact that the pregnancy had crossed the statutory limit under the Medical Termination of Pregnancy (MTP) Act could not, by itself, be considered in isolation in cases arising from sexual assault.'15-year-old cannot be reduced to description of mother'Justice Jain said courts exercising jurisdiction under Articles 226 or 32 of the Constitution must give due primacy to the best interests and welfare of the minor, while also taking into account the statutory framework under the MTP Act.The court described the case as "unfortunate and distressing", noting that the girl was only 15, had already suffered the trauma of an alleged heinous sexual assault and had lost both her parents."A child of 15 years cannot, in the eyes of this court, be reduced to the description of a 'mother' merely because she has been forced into pregnancy as a consequence of sexual violence," it said.The court said that while the law could provide remedies and procedures, no judicial order could undo the trauma the child had endured.Allowing the plea, the court directed the medical superintendent of Lady Hardinge Medical College and S K Hospital to arrange for termination of the pregnancy at the earliest and maintain a record of the procedure.The doctors were also directed to preserve the tissue or foetal material for DNA identification and other purposes in connection with the criminal case registered over the rape.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Two dead after car hits group of pedestrians in Doncaster
articles.summary: A vehicle hit four people before colliding with two cars on White Rose Way in Doncaster, police say.
articles.body:
Two people have died and four have been seriously injured after a car crashed into a group of people in Doncaster.

South Yorkshire Police said officers were called to White Rose Way when a black Mitsubishi L200 hit a group of pedestrians at 11:00 BST on Sunday, before hitting a black Audi and silver BMW on the opposite carriageway.

The force said two of the pedestrians had died at the scene while four other people were taken to hospital with serious injuries.

The driver of the Mitsubishi, a 30-year-old man, was arrested on suspicion of two counts of causing death by dangerous driving, two counts of causing serious injury by dangerous driving and driving while unfit and later released on bail.

A police spokesperson said they were still "working to identify and inform" the families of those killed in the collision.

Anyone who witnessed the crash, which took place between Carriage Drive and Middle Bank Roundabout, or who has dashcam footage is asked to contact South Yorkshire Police.

articles.title: Guernsey records highest levels of air travel since 2019
articles.summary: Guernsey Ports said passengers numbers exceeding 75,000 in July for the first time since 2019.
articles.body:
Guernsey Ports saw the highest levels of air travel in seven years, bosses have said.

They said July was the busiest month at the island's airport so far this year, with passengers numbers exceeding 75,000 for the first time since 2019.

Staff also said sea travel had also recorded a consecutive year-on-year increase.

Ports managing director Ross Coppolo said the figures showed the continued appeal of Guernsey as a destination and the importance of maintaining reliable connections for residents.

Ports said there was also growth across ferry services, with passenger numbers on Guernsey's northern and southern sea routes 3% higher than July 2025.

It said August 2026 was a "quieter" month compared to 2025, but ferry travel remained ahead of 2024, with the overall year-to-date passenger numbers 1% up on 2025, which was itself 14% higher than the year before.

Private aviation "increased significantly" during 2026, with aircraft movements about 30% higher than the same period in 2025.

It said Guernsey's marina's continued to perform with visiting vessel and passenger numbers close to the high levels achieved the year previous.

It said year-end totals for visiting leisure craft were expected to be close to those from 2025, when about 7,800 private vessels brought about 20,000 visitors to the island.

Coppolo said it was "very encouraging to see continued growth" across both the airport and harbours.

He said: "These figures reflect the efforts of our teams and partners to strengthen connectivity and improve the customer experience for residents and visitors alike and demonstrates the sustained demand for travel to and from the bailiwick.

"Our focus remains on providing safe, efficient and dependable services while working with our partners to ensure the bailiwick remains well connected."

articles.title: Unions urge ministers to soften planned changes to immigration rules
articles.summary: The home secretary wants to double the time it takes for most migrants to qualify for permanent residence.
articles.body:
Trade unions are putting pressure on the government to soften proposed changes to immigration rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.

If the plans are approved, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for permanent residence, rather than five years, while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.

The proposals were announced last year by Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood , who has kept the same role under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Delegates at the Trades Union Congress (TUC) backed a motion calling for any changes affecting workers already in the UK to be withdrawn.

A government spokesperson said ministers had received 200,000 responses to a consultation on the proposals, which was launched under Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer, and they were carefully considering them.

Mahmood has previously defended the plans, saying the "unprecedented" number of people arriving in the UK demands an answer from the government.

Under the government's proposals the standard wait to qualify for settlement, also known as indefinite leave to remain, would increase to 10 years.

People who arrived on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait, while those who relied on benefits for more than 12 months would have to wait 20 years.

Indefinite leave to remain gives a person the right to live, work and study in the UK for as long as they like and apply for benefits if they are eligible.

The changes would not apply to people who have already obtained settlement but would cover people already living in the UK, including those who had been expecting to get permanent residence in the coming months.

Some Labour MPs have also criticised plans for the changes to apply to migrants already in the UK.

Earlier this year, when she was a backbench MP and not a government minister, Angela Rayner, herself a former care worker, labelled the proposals "un-British" .

Rayner, who has since been appointed housing secretary by Burnham, warned that "moving the goalposts undermines our sense of fair play".

At the time, Burnham, who was still Greater Manchester mayor, said he understood where Rayner was "coming from" and that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Don't change rules for migrants already in UK, Labour MPs tell Mahmood

Reform plans to scrap indefinite leave to remain for migrants

The UK's biggest union, Unison, called on delegates to agree they were "alarmed at sweeping attacks on migrant workers which render them second-class citizens in the UK".

Unison senior vice president Debbie Rowden said the plans would drive away international staff despite shortages in critical roles, including in the care sector, where the qualification period would treble.

"The government wants to give bankers a three-year route to settlement, but social care workers will be kept waiting for 15 years," she said.

"The same for nursing auxiliaries, theatre nurses, health care assistants, children's residential care workers, probation service workers and more.

"What does this say about how public service workers are valued? What does this say about the soul of the country, when health and social care is seen as being a low contributor, but bankers as the highest?"

The Society of Radiographers seconded the motion, setting out how international technician numbers had plugged major gaps in NHS workforces, but that numbers had fallen 12% by more than 1,500 between January and March this year because "the goalposts had moved" on settlement.

The motion, which also called for the five-year route to settlement to be retained for workers, was passed unanimously by delegates.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Diana, Princess of Wales: "I'd like to be a queen in people's hearts, but I don't see myself being…" - lesson about redefining influence
articles.summary: UK News: Two people can be told their formal path to influence has narrowed or closed entirely and respond in completely different ways. One treats the loss of.
articles.body: Two people can be told their formal path to influence has narrowed or closed entirely and respond in completely different ways. One treats the loss of the expected title or position as the end of any real influence at all, and withdraws accordingly. The other redefines what influence actually means for them, choosing a different, less official kind of standing that doesn't depend on the position they were originally meant to hold. Diana said this line during her explosive BBC Panorama interview with Martin Bashir in November 1995, at a point when her marriage to Prince Charles had publicly and irreversibly broken down and her eventual path to the British throne, as queen consort, was no longer realistic. Rather than treating that loss as the end of her public relevance, she reframed the entire premise, trading a formal, inherited title for something she considered to be won through direct emotional connection instead.Quote of the day by Princess Diana"I'd like to be a queen in people's hearts, but I don't see myself being queen of this country."Written during the interview that changed how the public saw herWhat gives this line its full weight is the interview it came from, one of the most consequential television appearances in modern royal history. Broadcast to an audience of over 20 million people in the UK alone, the Panorama interview saw Diana speak with unusual candour about the state of her marriage, famously remarking that "there were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded," a direct reference to Charles's relationship with Camilla Parker-Bowles, and discussing her own struggles with bulimia and self-harm during a period when the royal family offered her little public support.Against that backdrop, the "queen of people's hearts" line reads less like a consolation prize and more like a genuine redefinition of her role. In the years following the interview and her 1996 divorce, Diana leaned heavily into humanitarian work that relied on exactly the kind of direct, personal connection she was describing, including her prominent campaign against landmines and her decision, at a time when public fear and stigma around HIV and AIDS ran high, to be photographed shaking hands, without gloves, with a man dying of the disease in 1987, a gesture credited with helping shift public attitudes. The formal title never arrived. The informal one, by most accounts of how she was regarded by the public at the time of her death in 1997, largely did.A simple way to actually use this ideaThe useful move here is separating the specific, formal version of a goal from the underlying thing that goal was actually meant to provide, since losing access to the first doesn't necessarily mean losing access to the second. A closed door to an official title, promotion, or position doesn't have to mean the influence, connection, or respect that position represented is now permanently out of reach. A fair test, when an expected path forward closes off, is to ask what the position was actually supposed to provide, and whether there's a different, less conventional route to that same underlying thing. That question won't undo a genuine loss. It usually reveals more available paths forward than the closed door initially seemed to leave.Other quotes by Princess Diana:"There were three of us in this marriage, so it was a bit crowded." "Whoever is in distress can call on me. I will come running, wherever they are." "I think every strong woman in history has had to walk down a similar path, and I think it's the strength that causes the confusion and the fear."Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Shin Bet, police arrest central Israel resident for planning October 7-inspired terror attack
articles.summary: The suspect was reportedly inspired by the October 7 massacre and was planning on carrying out a terrorist attack involving explosives. A 19-year-old residen...
articles.body:
Israeli authorities arrested a 19-year-old resident of Kafr Kassem for planning a terrorist attack inspired by a previous massacre.

The suspect was found in possession of training equipment, airsoft weapons, and materials to manufacture explosive devices.

The investigation revealed that the suspect had involved others in his attempts to create homemade explosives for terror attacks.

The suspect was reportedly inspired by the October 7 massacre and was planning on carrying out a terrorist attack involving explosives.

A 19-year-old resident of Kafr Kassem was arrested on suspicion of advancing terrorist activity and planning to carry out an attack, the Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) and the Israel Police stated on Tuesday.

The joint investigation found that Issa had been influenced by the October 7 massacre . According to the investigation, he subsequently began advancing a plan to carry out a terrorist attack .

When Issa was arrested, investigators found a large amount of training equipment and airsoft weapons in his possession. His interrogation further revealed that he had used his cellphone to search for combat manuals and had downloaded and saved guides dealing with the manufacture of explosive devices.

Suspect learned how to create homemade explosives in preparation for terror attacks

According to the investigation's findings, the suspect did not limit himself to searching for information. The Shin Bet and police allege that he attempted to manufacture explosive devices using various materials and also involved other people in those attempts.

Following his interrogations by the Shin Bet and the Sharon Central Unit, prosecutors submitted a declaration to the Central District Court ahead of filing an indictment against him.

Public hearings over the future of a huge proposed solar farm are due to get under way.

Developer Island Green Power (IGP) has said the East Pye scheme will be on land near Long Stratton, in Norfolk, and will generate enough power for 115,000 homes.

Six months of hearings, starting on Tuesday at Dunston Hall, near Norwich, will examine the scheme spanning 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares).

Once this examination process has ended, inspector David Cliff will have three months to submit a recommendation to the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, who will have a further three months to make a decision.

The project will stretch across a number of villages including Hempnall, Great Moulton and Saxlingham Nethergate.

However, the plans have previously been strongly opposed by residents and campaign groups concerned about the loss of agricultural land and impact on the countryside.

The Local Democracy Reporting Service said almost 2,000 people had made representations during the consultation phase, with many vehemently opposed to the project.

In documents submitted to the government, IGP estimated the solar farm would cost £1bn to build .

This figure includes land acquisition, construction and installation costs.

Due to its size, the solar farm project is considered nationally significant and is one of three major solar farms planned for Norfolk.

Hearings for The Droves solar farm near Swaffham are already under way, while the High Grove solar farm, proposed near Dereham, is in the pre-application phase.

East Pye's first hearing on Tuesday will set out the examination process and will include an open hearing where people registered to speak can make representations.

Another open floor hearing will take place on Wednesday, with more than 60 people including MPs and councillors registered to speak.

Further hearings have been pencilled in for November and December and the examination is expected to end in February.
